text: Every request to the Kubernetes API server — kubectl, a controller, a webhook — passes through three stages in order. Authentication asks who you are, checked against client certificates, bearer or ServiceAccount tokens, or an external OIDC provider. Authorization asks whether that identity may perform the action, combining RBAC with the Node authorizer, which limits what a kubelet can touch. Admission control runs last, and even an authorized request can still be rejected or mutated there.

Admission controllers run as a chain, and a handful matter most in production. NodeRestriction stops a compromised kubelet's credentials from relabeling itself into a more privileged pool or editing other nodes' objects. PodSecurity enforces the standards from the last lesson. ResourceQuota and LimitRanger cap what a namespace can consume. They're layered on top of RBAC, not a replacement — authorization decides if you're allowed to ask; admission decides if the ask itself is acceptable.

The API server can log every request it receives, controlled by an audit policy that sets a detail level per rule. None means don't log. Metadata records who, what, and when with no body. RequestResponse captures the full request and response — the most detail, but expensive, and risky on anything that returns Secret contents. Wire it in with an audit policy file and a log path, and in an incident that log is often the only record of who actually touched what.

Every object in the cluster lives in etcd — every Secret, every ConfigMap, every Deployment spec. By default what's stored there is only base64-encoded, and base64 is an encoding, not a cipher — anyone with raw access to the data directory or a snapshot can read every Secret in plain text. An EncryptionConfiguration resource fixes that, telling the API server to encrypt specific resource types, Secrets especially, before they're ever written to etcd.

Encryption alone isn't the whole story. etcd should never be reachable outside the control plane network — only the API server talks to it directly, over mutual TLS, with its client and peer ports firewalled off from everything else. Back it up regularly with etcdctl snapshot save, but remember a snapshot of an unencrypted store is exactly as readable as the live database, so encryption has to be in place before that backup is worth anything.

Authentication, authorization, admission, audit, and an encrypted, access-restricted etcd — that's the control plane hardened end to end. Next lesson pulls everything from this chapter, RBAC, Pod Security Standards, and this one, into a single concrete checklist to run through before a cluster actually goes to production.
